"The story isn't landing"

By lowob · 7 September 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

When the story isn't landing, the deck is usually aimed at the wrong audience, built on a category word instead of a buyer, or hiding its evidence too late. Fix those three before touching anything else.

What it usually means

Founders hear "the story isn't landing" as a narrative problem. It rarely is. It is almost always one of three structural faults.

The first is audience. The deck was written for customers and is being shown to investors, or the reverse. Customers need to know what changes for them on Monday. Investors need to know why this becomes a large business and why you are the team to build it. One deck cannot carry both jobs. When it tries, each reader gets half of what they came for.

The second is the product truth. Read the one-liner on slide 1. If it says "a platform for X" or "the leading Y for Z", there is a category word where a buyer should be. Categories are for analysts. Investors fund a named buyer with a named problem and a reason to pay now.

The third is evidence placement. The best non-founder proof, a paying customer, a renewal, a partner that shipped, sits on slide 9. By then the reader has sat through market size, trend slides and a vision statement. Attention is gone before the proof arrives.

Where it traces to

This traces to Part 2 and Part 3 of the series.

Part 2 said one product truth, one belief per audience, and a claims register. If the deck does not land, check whether the truth has a buyer in it and whether a belief was ever written for the investor. Most decks skip that step and hope the product sells itself.

Part 3 said raise against evidence, not narrative. The evidence log exists so you can lead with the strongest organic proof. If the log is thin, or full of incentivised signals, the deck will feel like narrative no matter how well it is written. That is a different problem, and Part 37 will cover it.

The first move this week

Three moves, in order. Each takes an afternoon.

Move What changes Why it works
Evidence to slide 2 Best non-founder proof follows the title Reader believes before they are asked to imagine
Rewrite the truth Remove the category word, insert the buyer and the problem Investor can repeat it to a partner without notes
One investor belief A single sentence they must accept to invest Every slide either proves it or gets cut

Start with the evidence. Pull the log from Part 3. Pick the one item a sceptic would find hardest to dismiss. Put it on slide 2, with a number and a date if you have them, and nothing else on the slide.

Then the truth. Write it as "we help [buyer] do [thing] so that [outcome]". Resist the urge to sound bigger. Specific reads as credible.

Then the belief. Write it down, then walk the deck and mark each slide as proof, context or filler. Cut the filler. Move the context behind the proof.

Send the revised deck to the next two meetings only. Compare the questions you get with the questions you were getting before.

What not to do

Do not add market slides. The investor already knows the market exists or they would not have taken the meeting.

Do not hire a deck designer. Design makes a clear story cleaner. It cannot find a buyer that is not there.

Do not change the valuation. A price cut on a story that is not landing tells the investor you are not sure either. Fix the story, then talk about terms.

How you know it worked

Two signs. First, the questions in meetings shift from "help me understand what this is" to "how do you get more of these customers". Second, at least one investor repeats your truth back to you in their own words, correctly, without looking at the deck.

The checklist

Best non-founder evidence is on slide 2, with a date.

Product truth names a buyer and a problem, with no category word.

One investor belief written down, and every remaining slide proves it.

lowob takeaways

  • One deck cannot serve both customers and investors; each reader gets half of what they came for.
  • Move the best non-founder proof, with a number and date, to slide 2.
  • Do not add market slides, hire a deck designer or cut the valuation to fix a story that isn't landing.
